⚡ The KV Cache Quantization Rule: When to Use It (and When NOT To)

Baseline Recommendation: Default to unquantized (FP16/BF16) KV cache whenever VRAM allows. Every primary context limit listed in the matrix below assumes full-precision KV cache.

Quantizing the KV cache to FP8 or FP4 halves or quarters its memory footprint, but it introduces numerical noise into the attention mechanisms. Whether that degradation matters depends entirely on the workload:

  • When you SHOULD NOT quantize KV Cache:

    • Agentic Coding & Repo Editing: Quantized KV cache introduces subtle token hallucinations, misses syntax rules, and breaks multi-hop file references.
    • Deterministic Logic, Math & Deep Reasoning: Attention sinks and drift cause chain-of-thought models to lose coherence during long generation steps.
    • Needle-in-a-Haystack (NIAH) & Technical RAG: Critical facts buried in large documents are often skipped or misattributed once context scales past 32k tokens.

  • When KV Cache Quantization IS Acceptable:

    • Creative Writing & Long-Form Fiction: Gist and narrative momentum matter more than verbatim recall. Minor attention drift rarely breaks a story.
    • Casual Chatbots & Roleplay: Conversational flow is tolerant of minor precision loss.
    • VRAM-Constrained Exploration: When stretching a card beyond its native capacity is the only way to run a task, and fuzzy recall is acceptable.
    • Batch/Unattended Workloads: When throughput-per-dollar matters more than per-token precision (e.g., overnight document translation, large-scale summarization).

If a workload requires precision, scale context via model weight quantization (such as AutoRound W4A16) combined with RoPE/YaRN (if going over the native model context), while keeping the KV cache in native FP16/BF16.

🖥️ Hardware Vendor Notes (NVIDIA / AMD / Apple)

Easiest start on any platform: Unsloth Desktop is the recommended all-in-one app — it runs GGUF, safetensors, and FP8 models on NVIDIA CUDA, AMD ROCm/Vulkan, Intel Vulkan, and Apple Metal/MLX, with chat, no-code fine-tuning, and an OpenAI-compatible API server built in. Ollama and LM Studio remain solid lighter-weight alternatives if you prefer minimal overhead.

NVIDIA (CUDA)

All models in this matrix are tested and verified on NVIDIA hardware. W4A16 AutoRound quants require compute capability 7.0+ (Turing or newer). FP8 weights require 8.9+ (Ada/Hopper). Multi-GPU tensor parallelism works out of the box with vLLM and llama.cpp.

AMD (ROCm / Vulkan)

Fully supported via llama.cpp (ROCm backend for gfx906+, Vulkan for older) and vLLM (ROCm builds). Key notes:

  • Radeon VII (gfx906, 16GB HBM2): Excellent for ≤16GB tier models. Community-verified at 54–96 tok/s decode on Q4 models. HBM2 bandwidth (800 GB/s) makes it competitive with RTX 3060 12GB for inference.
  • RX 7900 XT (gfx1100, 20GB): Sits in the 16–24GB tier.
  • RX 7900 XTX (gfx1100, 24GB): Full ROCm support. Handles 24–32GB tier comfortably.
  • MI210 / MI250 / MI300X: Datacenter cards. MI210 is FP16-only (no FP8), so W4A16 AutoRound is the optimal quant. 4x MI210 = 256GB VRAM.
  • llama-swap is the recommended container for AMD multi-model serving (see community data below).
Apple (Metal / Unified Memory)

Unified memory means VRAM = system RAM. A 64GB Mac Studio can run models that need 48–64GB “VRAM” since there’s no separate GPU memory wall. Metal backend in llama.cpp and MLX for native Apple Silicon inference. No tensor parallelism needed — single GPU address space.

📦 Running Non-GGUF Models (AutoRound / Safetensors / FP8)

AutoRound W4A16 models are not single .GGUF files. They are distributed as HuggingFace Safetensors shards (typically 4–10 files) and require a compatible inference backend:

Option A: vLLM (Recommended for W4A16 AutoRound)

pip install vllm

vllm serve <huggingface-repo-id> \
  --quantization auto-round-w4a16 \
  --max-model-len 262144 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 \
  --port 8000

Option B: llama.cpp (for GGUF alternatives)

If you prefer llama.cpp, look for the GGUF quant of the same base model (e.g., unsloth/<model>-GGUF). You lose the AutoRound optimization but gain single-file portability and broader hardware support (Vulkan, Metal, CPU offload).

Option C: LM Studio / Ollama

These tools primarily support GGUF. For AutoRound W4A16, use vLLM directly or check if the model author has published a GGUF conversion.

Option D: Unsloth Desktop (All-in-One)

Unsloth Desktop natively supports GGUF, safetensors, FP8, and MLX formats, with llama.cpp as the core engine and vLLM as the deployment backend. It works on NVIDIA CUDA, AMD ROCm/Vulkan, Intel Vulkan, and Apple Metal/MLX — one app for any package format in this matrix.

Emerging: NVFP4 / MXFP4

The next frontier in 4-bit quantization. NVFP4 (NVIDIA) and MXFP4 (microscaling, cross-vendor) offer better quality-per-bit than W4A16 AutoRound or GGUF Q4_K_M, with native hardware acceleration on Blackwell (RTX 50xx) and upcoming MI300/MI400 chips. Community consensus (Strawberry, lhl): “NVFP4 → MXFP4 is the real golden ticket” — Flash-Next in NVFP4 is already the top pick at the 96-128GB tier. Expect these formats to dominate the matrix within 6-12 months as more models ship native MXFP4 checkpoints.

⚠️ Technical Architecture Note: Qwen Flash-Next N-gram Lookahead & Memory Offload

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (and the Swift-1.5 fine-tune) implements a high-throughput n-gram lookahead speculative table. This structure requires approximately 95 GB of unquantized index memory in addition to the ~73 GB base W4A16 model weights:

  1. Host RAM Offload Mode (Tier 5 / 96-128 GB VRAM):
    • VRAM Allocation: Only the ~73 GB model weights live on the GPUs.
    • System RAM Requirement: The ~95 GB n-gram table is mapped directly to pinned host memory over PCIe. Your host machine must have at least 128 GB of system RAM.
    • Bus Requirement: PCIe Gen4 x4, PCIe Gen3 x8 or higher per card is strongly recommended to prevent host-to-device speculative verification latency from bottlenecking token throughput.
  2. Pure VRAM Mode (Tier 6 / 196+ GB VRAM):
    • VRAM Allocation: Can load both the weights (~73 GB) and the n-gram table (~95 GB) entirely in GPU memory, consuming ~168 GB of static VRAM before allocating the first token of KV cache.

Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next inherits this architecture. The Swift fine-tune modifies the language model weights but retains the n-gram speculative table structure, so the same offload considerations apply.

Physical Space 8-GPU rigs need 8U+ racks or large ATX cases. Consumer builds top out at 2-4 GPUs practically. Tier 5-6 Server chassis, blade enclosures, or Mac Studio (dense unified memory).
OS / Driver Maturity ROCm lags CUDA by 6-12 months for new features. Vulkan is universal but slower. Metal is Apple-only. All tiers NVIDIA = easiest. AMD = great for inference, harder for training. Apple = zero-config but limited to Apple models.

Community Submissions, Hardware Feedback & Thread Evolution

Rather than running rigid polls right out of the gate, this thread is designed to gather real-world, operational data from the community. Automated benchmarks and leaderboards miss how setups actually behave day-to-day — I want to know what you’re actually loading up, what you use it for, and how you have it tuned.

Use this space to share your daily drivers, niche workflow solutions, hardware limits, and suggestions on how to improve this living guide.

Quick Navigation:

  • 🌱 Start Here: New to Local LLMs?
  • 📝 What I Want to Hear From You
  • 📋 Submission Templates (Quick + Full)
  • ⚙️ Backend Selection Guide
  • 🧰 Supporting Software (see Post #1)
  • 💡 Thread Feedback & Suggested Changes
  • ✅ Example Submissions
🌱 Start Here: New to Local LLMs? (Decision Flow)

A quick path from “I want to run a local AI” to “I know what to buy and how to set it up.” Follow the questions that match your situation.

Q1: What’s your budget?

  • Under $500 (used/entry): Look at Tier 1. A used RTX 3060 12GB or RX 7600 8GB gets you started. You'll run 7-9B models at Q4. Expect 20-40 tok/s. Start with Ollama + LM Studio for zero-config ease.
  • $500–$1,500 (single modern GPU): Tier 1-2. RTX 4060 Ti 16GB, RX 7900 XT 20GB, or RTX 4080 16GB. You can run 27B models at Q4/W4A16. This is the sweet spot for most hobbyists.
  • $1,500–$4,000 (high-end single or dual): Tier 3. RTX 4090 24GB, RX 7900 XTX 24GB, or 2x mid-range cards. Full 27B models with serious context.
  • $4,000–$15,000 (multi-GPU workstation): Tier 4-5. 2-4x high-end GPUs. Production-grade serving, multi-client, extreme context.
  • $15,000+ (server/enterprise): Tier 6. 8+ GPUs or Mac Studio Ultra. Running 70B+ models, multimodal, full speculative decoding stacks.
  • Any budget + lots of RAM (hybrid): With Strata, a single 24GB GPU + 128GB system RAM can run 125B+ MoE models at 100+ tok/s. You don't need massive VRAM if you have fast RAM and NVMe. This changes the game for consumer builds.

Q2: What do you want to DO with it?

  • Chat / general assistant: Tier 1 is fine. Qwen3.5-4B or Ornith-1.5-9B. Fast, cheap, always-on.
  • Coding / agentic workflows: Tier 2 minimum. Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27b is the community pick. You need 256k context for real repo work.
  • Creative writing / roleplay: Tier 1-2. Gemma-4 models excel here. KV quantization is acceptable.
  • Research / RAG / document analysis: Tier 3+. You need FP16/BF16 KV cache and 100k+ context.
  • Production serving (multiple users): Tier 4+. vLLM with multi-GPU tensor parallelism.

Q3: What’s your comfort level?

  • "I just want it to work": Unsloth Desktop. Download it, pick a model from the built-in hub, chat. No commands, no configs, no terminal. You'll be up in 5 minutes. It handles GGUF, safetensors, and FP8 models, works on NVIDIA/AMD/Apple, and gives you an OpenAI-compatible API server for free. (Ollama and LM Studio are lighter alternatives if you want minimal overhead.)
  • "I'm comfortable with a terminal": llama.cpp directly, or Ollama with custom models. You can tune context, quantization, and sampling params.
  • "I want maximum performance": vLLM with AutoRound W4A16 or FP8 quants. Continuous batching, PagedAttention, speculative decoding. Steeper learning curve, best throughput.
    • For AMD: Radiance gives you 200+ tok/s with MTP on R9700s.
    • For hybrid offload: Strata turns a single GPU + big RAM into a 125B model runner.
  • "I'm building a product": vLLM + LiteLLM proxy + Docker. Multi-model routing, load balancing, API-compatible serving.

Q4: NVIDIA, AMD, or Apple?

  • NVIDIA: Easiest path. Every backend supports it. CUDA is the reference implementation. If you're new, start here.
  • AMD: Great value. ROCm works well for inference (llama.cpp, vLLM). Slightly steeper setup. Best $/VRAM ratio for multi-GPU.
  • Apple: Zero-config unified memory. A $4K Mac Studio gives you 64GB "VRAM." No multi-GPU scaling, but incredible simplicity. MLX is the native framework, and Unsloth Desktop supports Apple Silicon via MLX out of the box.

Still stuck? Post in the thread with your budget and use case. The community will point you to the right tier and model.

📝 What I Want to Hear From You

Whether you’re pushing multi-GPU tensor parallelism in headless servers or running daily local workflows on consumer cards and unified memory laptops, chime in on:

  1. What model & quantization do you actually rely on? AutoRound W4A16, GGUF Q4_K_M / IQ4_XS, native FP8, unquantized BF16, EXL2 4.0bpw — whatever you've dialled in.
  2. What is your primary use case? Agentic coding, large repo ingestion, technical RAG, multi-step math/logic, casual chat, long-form creative writing, document translation, security research.
  3. How are you serving it?
    • Backend / runtime: vLLM, direct llama.cpp, LM Studio, Ollama, Unsloth Desktop, llama-swap, Colibri, etc.
    • Architecture: Single GPU, multi-GPU split (tensor parallel or row/layer offloading), host RAM offloading, CPU+GPU hybrid, custom RoPE/YaRN factors, speculative decoding (MTP / n-gram).
    • OS / Driver: Linux (which distro), Windows, macOS. CUDA, ROCm, Vulkan, Metal.
  4. Context & KV behavior Did you keep the KV cache unquantized (FP16/BF16), or did you drop to FP8/INT4? Where does the model hold coherence versus fall apart? What's your tested stable context limit?
  5. Performance numbers (optional but valuable) Decode tok/s, prefill tok/s, TTFT (cold load), power draw (W), GPU utilization %.
📋 Submission Templates (Quick + Full)

To keep submissions consistent and allow aggregation into the Master Matrix (Post #1), pick the format that matches how much detail you want to share:

Quick Submit (30 seconds):

[QUICK-SUBMIT]
gpu: [Your GPU model + VRAM]
model: [Model name + quant]
use_case: [What you use it for]
verdict: [One sentence: does it work? any quirks?]
[/QUICK-SUBMIT]

That’s it. If you have 30 seconds, this is enough to get your data into the matrix. No template gymnastics required.

Use Quick Submit for casual reports. Use Full Submit when you have benchmark numbers, context test results, or specific launch configs you want captured in the matrix.

Full Submit (for detailed data):

(You don’t have to fill out every line if you’re just dropping casual thoughts, but using the structured block makes it easy to integrate your numbers directly into the master matrix. New fields: os_driver, weight_precision, prefill_tps, ttft_cold, power_draw — all optional but help with hardware-specific recommendations. (New optional field: engine_mode — specifies whether your setup is pure VRAM, hybrid offload (Strata-style), or CPU+GPU. This helps the matrix accurately represent what’s actually running where.)

⚙️ Backend Selection Guide — Which Runtime Should You Use?

The model is only half the equation. How you serve it determines your speed, features, and flexibility.
